units.translation: which Hesychius, no doubt from this passage, explains by ἀπάνθρωπον [inhospitable], as Aeschylus himself said in v. 20 απανθρώπῳ πάγῳ [on an inhospitable crag]. The reading interpolated in M, ἄβατόν τ' [and inaccessible] (τ' rightly deleted in the copies), which the scholiast also used on v. 15, was corrected from the scholium on Homer Il. 14, 78 βροτὸς γὰρ καὶ ὁ φώς. καὶ Αἰσχύλος “ἄβροτον εἰς ἐρημίαν”, δῆλον ἐν ᾗ φώς οὐ γίνεται [for brotos is also a man. And Aeschylus: "into an untrodden solitude," clearly where no man comes]. In the scholium on Aristophanes Frogs 827 (copied by Suidas under the word ἐριβρεμέτας) ἄβροτον is in codex Ven. 474, but ἄβατον in Rav. and in the copy of Venetus, Veneto 475. In Suidas ἄβατον in the inferior books, ἄβροτον in the best. ἄβατον also in Synesius Epist. p. 35.

epithet transferred to the soft and luxurious coverlets of Persian women.
Persian women – having abandoned the soft-tunicked beds, the delight of delicate youth,
ἁβρύνομαι to behave delicately, to be proud, to grow insolent
and do not pamper me in the ways of a woman.
for every man who fares well becomes proud.
lacking a bottom, i.e. very deep, immense. Figuratively
Why should I delay to look upon the divine mind, a bottomless sight?
and beneath the body of the earth there will be boundless wealth.
The middle form has various meanings in Homer and others; the active is rare, noted by Hesychius and Etym. M. p. 5, 30 ἀγάζει: ἀγανακτεῖ, βαρέως φέρει [agazei: he is vexed, he bears heavily].

Similarly Soph. OC. 1695 τὸ φέρον ἐκ θεοῦ καλῶς μηδὲν ἄγαν φλέγεσθον [bear well what comes from god, do not burn excessively], which the scholium explains as μὴ ἄκρως φλέγεσθε τὸ ἐκ Θεοῦ πεμφθὲν δυσανασχέτως φέρουσαι [do not burn excessively, bearing what is sent from God with impatience]. But more apt for Aeschylus' verse is the scholiast's interpretation λίαν ἐξετάζειν [to examine too much], to inquire curiously, which is supported by the preceding words cited under the word ἄβυσσος. The active ἀγάζεις from Sophocles (fr. 797) is noted in Bekk. Anecd. p. 336, 6, where it is explained by θρασύνεις [you are bold].
SEMICHORUS. What occasion do you teach me? SEMICHORUS. Not to be vexed at the things of the gods.

good, mostly of persons, but often also of things. Since the notion of good is broad, it can often be rendered by more specific adjectives, such as στρατιά ἀγαθή [a brave army] said of a strong army, τύχη ἀγαθή [good fortune].
